images.title: Is the doubt pointing at something real?
images.alt: Decision chart: if you can name what you need to do before publishing, do it; if you can't and the post is accurate, publish it.
images.caption: Useful doubt points at a specific gap. Vague doubt about an accurate post is a reason to publish.

data.question: Can you name what you'd need to do to feel ready to publish this post?

branches.result: Do it: check the claim, try the step, or rework the section you don't understand.
If the post is accurate and honest about what you know, publish it.

images.after: "Who am I to write about this?" has a practical answer
images.title: Claim only what's true
images.alt: Four cards: write from what you've done, say what you have and haven't tested, document instead of posing, and be honest about your level.
images.caption: You feel like a fraud when a post implies more than you can back up, so close the gap from that side.

items.title: Write from what you did
items.text: "How I set up my first blog" is a post you're fully qualified to write

items.title: Say what you tested
items.text: If you only read the documentation, say so

items.title: Document, don't pose
items.text: What you tried, what happened and what you'd do differently

items.title: State your level
items.text: One line on how long you've done this and where your information comes from

images.after: Habits that make the feeling quieter over time
images.title: Habits that build evidence
images.alt: Checklist of five habits: publish small, narrow the topic, keep a record of reader replies, compare against your own earlier work, and fix mistakes openly.
images.caption: These don't make the doubt disappear. They give it evidence to respond to.

items: Publish small: one narrow question per post
Narrow the topic until you know it completely
Save reader replies that say a post helped
Compare your tenth post with your first, not with other creators
Fix mistakes in the open and note the update
